variants.name: Closures with iterator adapters
variants.idiom_name: Fn(&T) -> bool closures composed in iterator pipelines
variants.implementation_notes: Rust's rule is a closure behind the Fn traits: `let overdue = |i: &Invoice| i.days_past_due >= 30;` and composition is either a closure over the parts or a small generic combinator, consumed by Iterator::filter/all/any or Option::filter. Generic parameters (`fn matching<'a, T, P: Fn(&T) -> bool>(items: impl IntoIterator<Item = &'a T>, spec: P)`) keep the pipeline monomorphized with no allocation and no dynamic dispatch. The named-trait form (trait Specification<T> { fn is_satisfied_by(&self, candidate: &T) -> bool; } plus And/Or/Not structs) is warranted when rules are stored in collections, chosen at runtime, sent across threads, or translated into a query; the enum form is warranted when the rule tree must be serialized or rendered - those two are the sibling variants.
pitfalls: Every closure has a unique anonymous type, so rules cannot be stored in a homogeneous collection or named in a struct field without boxing or an enum ('expected closure, found a different closure').
A closure borrowing captured state ties the rule's lifetime to that data; storing it requires a lifetime parameter or a move closure.
Option::filter takes a predicate by value rather than composing, so chaining filters deepens nesting instead of building one rule; combine the predicates instead.
Closures are not comparable or loggable: deduplication, equality and diagnostics need a named type.

variants.name: Box<dyn Specification<T>> combinator structs
variants.idiom_name: trait Specification<T> with And/Or/Not structs behind Box<dyn>
variants.implementation_notes: For rules chosen at runtime - plugin registries, configuration, vectors of heterogeneous rules - keep the trait: `trait Specification<T> { fn is_satisfied_by(&self, candidate: &T) -> bool; }` with And/Or/Not structs holding children (boxed, or generic parameters when the shape is static) and a blanket `impl<T, F: Fn(&T) -> bool> Specification<T> for F` so closures stand in wherever an owned rule is expected. The boxed form buys nameability, storage and dynamic composition at the cost of a heap allocation per node and one vtable dispatch per evaluation, plus explicit lifetime/Send/Sync bounds when rules borrow or cross threads.
pitfalls: dyn Specification<T> is unsized: every combinator boxes its children, so a deep rule tree allocates per node - use generic parameters where the shape is known at compile time.
Trait objects are not Send/Sync by default; a rule set moved to another thread needs the bounds spelled out on every boxed type.
Borrowing rules need an explicit lifetime on the trait object, and 'static bounds silently exclude them.
Without the blanket impl for Fn, every closure must be wrapped by hand; the orphan rule also stops other crates from implementing the trait for their own types if the trait is foreign.

variants.name: Enum rule tree evaluated by match
variants.idiom_name: enum Spec { ... And(Box<Spec>, Box<Spec>), Or(..), Not(..) } with a match evaluator
variants.implementation_notes: When rules must be built from data, logged, sent over a wire, or translated into another query language (SQL, an API filter), model the rule as a data enum with And/Or/Not nodes and give it a match-based evaluator. Unlike closures and trait objects, the tree is inspectable and Serialize/Deserialize can be derived, which is exactly what a query translator needs; the price is boilerplate per leaf, a closed set of leaves fixed at compile time, and an evaluator plus every translator that must be kept in sync.
pitfalls: Every new leaf edits the enum, the evaluator and every translator; exhaustive match makes the compiler find the evaluator but not the SQL renderer, which lives in another crate.
Boxed children put the tree on the heap and make immutable sharing awkward; an arena plus indices is the usual alternative when the tree is large or traversed often.
If a translator exists, the rule is defined twice (enum semantics plus SQL semantics) and the two can drift - the pattern's classic double-definition risk in its purest form.
